title: Eliminating anisotropy and unlocking ultra‑high strength in TA15 via  in‑situ  nitrogen microalloying during micro laser powder bed fusion
abstract: Abstract Titanium alloys are vital for lightweight aerospace structures. Yet their application in micro-architected components using laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is constrained by pronounced anisotropy and inadequate as-built strength, which typically requires post-processing. Here, we introduce an in-situ microalloying strategy using reactive micro-LPBF (µ-LPBF) for TA15 (Ti-6Al-2Zr-1Mo-1 V), supported by multiphysics modeling. This approach leverages nitrogen to simultaneously trigger isotropic grain refinement and activate synergistic strengthening mechanisms. Compared to the anisotropic pure Ar counterparts, optimized 5 vol% N 2  specimens exhibit superior isotropic mechanical responses tailored for micro-bearing environments: achieving a record-breaking ultimate compressive strength of 2266 MPa (vs. 1827 MPa) and a hardness of 5.58 GPa (vs. 4.09 GPa), while maintaining a high strain-to-failure of 22.9%. The enhanced performance originates from the multifaceted role of nitrogen: increasing the molten pool’s energy absorptivity and inducing an obvious constitutional supercooling related to a high growth restriction factor for promoting a columnar-to-equiaxed transition of prior β-grains. At the atomic level, interstitial nitrogen promotes dislocation multiplication and in-situ polygonization into low-angle grain boundaries while stimulating deformation twinning. This coordinated “Solid Solution + Recovery” pathway enhances strength-plasticity synergy, providing a post-processing-free strategy for manufacturing high-performance, isotropic titanium components.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Compared with high-entropy alloys [ 1 ,  2 ], superalloys [ 3 ,  4 ], and ultra-high temperature alloys [ 5 ], titanium alloys, renowned for their exceptional specific strength and corrosion resistance, are indispensable for critical aerospace components where weight savings and structural reliability are paramount [ 6 ]. Among them, the near-α TA15 alloy (Ti-6Al-2Zr-1Mo-1 V) is a preferred choice for high-performance aerospace structures due to its superior specific strength and thermal stability [ 7 ,  8 ]. In contrast with conventional methods, laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) offers unparalleled design freedom for fabricating complex, lightweight titanium components, presenting a transformative route for aerospace engineering [ 9 ,  10 ]. With the miniaturization of aerospace systems, there is a growing demand to utilize L-PBF for creating intricate micro-lattices or thin-walled stiffeners [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ]. In these micro-scale scenarios, the material often faces complex stress states dominated by local compression and buckling [ 14 ]. However, the full potential of LPBF-fabricated high-strength titanium alloys remains constrained by inherent microstructural limitations. The steep, directional thermal gradients could trigger the epitaxial growth of coarse columnar prior-β grains [ 15 ,  16 ]. This textured microstructure leads to severe mechanical anisotropy and insufficient as-built strength, posing a reliability risk for applications demanding uniform multidirectional performance [ 17 ,  18 ]. For instance, recent investigations on LPBF-processed high-strength titanium alloys have highlighted that the crystallographic texture of coarsened columnar β grains results in significant direction-dependent mechanical responses, such as variations in tensile strength and a shift in failure modes from ductile to brittle depending on the loading orientation [ 19 ].

To mitigate anisotropy and enhance strength, prevailing strategies rely on post-processing, process parameter optimization, or inoculation. Post-processing treatments, such as heat treatment or hot isostatic pressing, alleviate anisotropy but at the expense of grain coarsening and strength loss [ 20 ,  21 – 22 ]. Moreover, these additional steps contradict the ethos of rapid, near-net-shape manufacturing. Process parameter manipulation is only partially effective within the narrow processing windows of titanium alloys [ 23 ,  24 ]. While inoculation holds great potential to promote a columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET), it risks introducing extrinsic defects that act as stress concentrators [ 25 ,  26 ]. Thus, a streamlined, in-situ strategy capable of simultaneously achieving isotropic and ultra-high strength remains a critical unmet need.

In this context, micro-LPBF (µ-LPBF), with its minimized laser spot and ultra-high cooling rates, presents a promising avenue for strength enhancement [ 27 ,  28 – 29 ]. Paradoxically, its extreme thermal gradients would exacerbate columnar growth, intensifying anisotropy [ 30 ]. To resolve this dilemma, reactive atmosphere-based microalloying emerges as a transformative solution. The introduction of nitrogen (N 2 ) during µ-LPBF enables it to function as a potent interstitial strengthener and solidification modifier [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ]. It was reported that a trace of nitrogen doping induces a high growth restriction factor ( Q ), altering solidification kinetics to promote CET and disrupt the deleterious columnar texture [ 34 ]. The synergy of µ-LPBF and reactive nitrogen thus offers a compelling pathway to simultaneously break the anisotropy-strength trade-off. However, this approach requires precise control, as excessive nitrogen is more likely to induce embrittlement via the precipitation of TiN [ 35 ,  36 ], and the underlying mechanisms governing microstructural evolution in Ti alloys are also not fully elucidated.

Herein, we present a comprehensive study on the reactive µ-LPBF of TA15 alloy via in-situ N 2  microalloying. This work moves beyond phenomenological reporting by in-situ monitoring, high-fidelity multiphysics simulation, and multiscale characterization to decode process-structure-property relationships. An optimized 5 vol% N 2  atmosphere yields TA15 with exceptional isotropic mechanical properties without any post-processing, achieving an ultimate compressive strength exceeding 2.2 GPa while retaining significant plasticity. By systematically elucidating how nitrogen modulates molten-pool dynamics, triggers CET, and activates a unique “Solid Solution + Recovery” strengthening pathway involving in-situ polygonization and twinning, this work presents a comprehensive, physics-based strategy for the additive fabrication of isotropic titanium alloys with superior performance.

Specimens were fabricated using a custom-developed µ-LPBF system with a 25 μm laser spot diameter (Fig.  1 e). A hybrid gas delivery module, maintaining a nitrogen-argon mixture, established a stable atmospheric environment, preventing fluctuations in nitrogen concentration. It also incorporates a coaxial molten pool monitoring (MPM) subsystem to track multiple optical emissions from the molten pool surface, including temperature, metallic evaporation, and energy absorption during solidification. The manufacturing parameters in Table  2  ensured a desirable quality, with the part measuring 8 × 8 × 5 mm (Fig.  1 c) and having a relative density of ~  99.7%. A 67°-rotated zig-zag scanning strategy minimized residual stress (Fig.  1 d).

sections.heading: Mechanical characterization
paragraphs: Nanoindentation was conducted on a nanoindenter (Triboindenter, Hysitron, USA) with a Berkovich diamond tip (5000 µN, 10 s). Five indentations were performed for each condition to obtain the average hardness and modulus. Room-temperature compressive properties were evaluated under quasi-static loading (strain rate: 0.001/s) using a universal test instrument (Electropuls E1000, Instron, USA). For each fabrication condition, three cylindrical specimens ( Φ 2 × 4 mm) were compressed along the axis perpendicular to the building direction (BD) and another three along the axis parallel to BD to evaluate orientation-dependent cylindrical responses. The nitrogen content in as-fabricated specimens was quantified using an ONH analyzer (LECO ONH836, USA) via inert gas fusion-infrared conductivity detection.

In addition to the solid solution, a weak TiN (110) diffraction peak was detected solely on the XOY plane of the 10% N 2  specimen (Fig.  2 b), consistent with its characteristic pale golden-yellow hue (Fig.  1 c) [ 43 ]. In contrast, no discernible nitride peaks were found in the specimen interior. This, along with the homogeneous nitrogen distribution and absence of secondary phases observed via SEM/EDS on the inner XOZ surface (Fig.  S1 ) [ 31 ], indicates that nitrogen predominantly exists as an interstitial solid solution within the bulk material. The maximum measured nitrogen content (1.03 wt%) is well below its solubility limit in α-Ti (6.03 wt% [ 32 ]), further supporting complete dissolution. It is inferred that any transient in-situ TiN likely dissolved during repetitive thermal cycling, restricting their presence solely to the as-built surface. This is corroborated by the intensifying golden-yellow coloration with higher nitrogen content (Fig.  S2 ).

sections.heading: Microstructural evolution and crystallographic characteristics
paragraphs: With increasing nitrogen content, a distinct microstructural evolution was observed. The vertical elongation of parent β-grains parallel to the building direction (BD) was effectively inhibited, leading to a columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET, Fig.  3 a1–c1). The α′-martensite laths were oriented at ~ 45° to the prior β-grain boundaries, and transverse striations from molten pool overlap were also visible [ 44 ]. The Parallel SEM results shown in Fig.  3 a2–c2 confirm the formation of a refined and hierarchical microstructure, whose progressive evolution is associated with nitrogen-induced grain refinement and spatial constraints. As quantified in Table  S1 , α′-martensite variants are classified into four tiers by the dimensional characteristic [ 45 ]. The primary α′-martensite with the highest aspect ratio (AR) aligns along columnar grain boundaries, with intragranular nucleation terminating at these interfaces. Secondary variants, possessing a lower AR, orient either orthogonally or parallel to the primary ones. Tertiary α′-martensite featuring a further reduced AR resides within the inter-lath regions of secondary variants, accompanied by even finer fourth-tier laths between them [ 46 ]. This typical hierarchical structure results from successive thermal cycles during deposition, involving partial reversion and reprecipitation of prior martensite [ 47 ]. The detailed mechanism associated with the effect of nitrogen content is discussed in Sect.  4.3 .

Fig. 3 Cross-sectional microstructures of the as-built specimens (XOZ plane):  a1 – c1  Optical morphologies of pure Ar, 5% N 2 , and 10% N 2  specimens;  a2 – c2  corresponding detailed SEM images showing the staggered α′-martensite structure

The suppressed epitaxial growth, corresponding to the CET effect shown in Fig.  3 , is also supported by reconstructed β-phase pole figures (Fig.  S3 ). A strong 〈001〉β//BD fiber texture, a typical feature of L-PBFed titanium alloys [ 49 ], weakens significantly with N 2  addition. Thus, the maximum intensities of α′-texture drop from 4.80 (pure Ar) to 3.68 (5% N 2 ) and to 2.60 (10% N 2 ), confirming nitrogen-induced texture randomization that inherits the refined β-grain structure. Meanwhile, the grain refinement and CET effect are quantitatively confirmed by the maximum Feret diameter (MFD) analysis (Fig.  4 a4–c4). With increasing N 2 , the grain size decreases progressively and the morphology shifts toward an equiaxed shape, with average MFD declining from 3.95 μm (pure Ar) to 1.73 μm (5% N 2 ) and 1.69 μm (10% N 2 ). However, the present data reveal an apparent discrepancy. As shown in Fig.  S4  and Table  3 , the nitrogen doping increases the fraction of LAGB fraction (19.7% → 29.4% → 23.8%) but unexpectedly reduces FWHM (0.321 → 0.237 → 0.226) and average KAM (0.89° → 0.85° → 0.87°). This contrasts with some reports suggesting nitrogen uniformly increases dislocation density and microstrain [ 35 ,  50 ], while aligning with others indicating strain relief [ 33 ]. This discrepancy will be resolved in Sect.  4.3  through the integrated microstructural analysis.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: Nanoindentation tests associated with load-displacement profiles shown in Fig.  6 a reveal that increasing nitrogen content enhances resistance to plastic deformation. Corresponding hardness rises from 4.44 ± 0.23 GPa (pure Ar) to 5.58 ± 0.13 GPa (5% N 2 ) and 6.90 ± 0.23 GPa (10% N 2 ), which is consistent with solid solution strengthening reported in previous work [ 53 ]. Concurrently, the reduced elastic modulus ( E r ) increases from 121.99 ± 2.56 GPa to 128.28 ± 2.20 GPa and 137.49 ± 2.02 GPa, indicating that nitrogen effectively tunes material stiffness.

Microstructural evolution induced by nitrogen further translates into enhanced compressive properties. As shown in Fig.  6 b, the stress–strain curves under different atmospheres confirm a substantial increase in strength with nitrogen addition. While loading perpendicular to BD yields high ultimate compressive strength ( σ max ), the mechanical anisotropy is significantly reduced in nitrogen-containing specimens (Table  4 ). Regardless of orientation,  σ max  rises from 1800 to 2000 MPa (pure Ar) to 2200–2300 MPa (5% N 2 ) and further to 2300–2400 MPa (10% N 2 ). However, the 10% N 2  specimens show a sharp drop in strain-to-failure ( ε f ) and compressive plastic strain ( ε p ), whereas the 5% N₂ condition achieves an optimal balance between strength and plasticity. As shown in Fig.  6 c, the present as-fabricated TA15 achieves a better strength-plasticity balance than the reported TA15 composites [ 54 ,  55 ,  56 ,  57 ,  58 – 59 ]. Given the comparable base properties of TA15 and TC4, the performance also surpasses that of L-PBFed TC4 fabricated under similar N 2 -Ar mixed atmospheres [ 35 ,  50 ,  60 ].

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Results mentioned above elucidate the multi-faceted role of nitrogen as a potent microstructural and performance modifier in the TA15 alloy fabricated via µ-LPBF. Nitrogen fundamentally alters molten-pool dynamics and energy absorption, which, in turn, governs solidification behavior, promotes a CET effect, and refines the hierarchical martensitic structure. Meanwhile, its interstitial solid solution induces significant lattice distortion and activates defect-mediated accommodation mechanisms. These coordinated microstructural evolutions underpin enhanced strength and tailored stiffness, demonstrating a coupled process-structure-property relationship enabled by in-situ atmosphere engineering. These interrelated mechanisms are discussed in detail in the following sections.

sections.heading: Effects of nitrogen on the molten-pool dynamics of µ-LPBF
paragraphs: In this work, optical signatures from the applied coaxial MPM provide insights into the effects of nitrogen doping on molten-pool status and process stability. As shown in Fig.  7 , nitrogen addition increases the intensities of both infrared and visible radiation. The infrared enhancement stems from laser‑nitrogen interactions. Specifically, nitrogen photoionization generates a transient, high‑electron‑density plasma [ 61 ], whose higher inverse‑bremsstrahlung absorption coefficient (compared to Ar) promotes the efficient energy transfer to the melt via electron‑phonon coupling. Driven by the strong chemical affinity between molten Ti and nitrogen, nitrogen dissolves at the interface and is rapidly carried into the melt pool by Marangoni and convective flows, a process that improves overall thermal transport [ 33 ]. This rapid liquid mixing, coupled with the ultra-high cooling rates inherent to µ-LPBF, is theoretically expected to induce a profound solute trapping effect. Such extreme kinetic conditions would significantly restrict time-dependent solute partitioning, favoring the retention of the dispersed nitrogen within the primary α′ lattice while minimizing massive localized segregation [ 62 ]. While precise micro-scale verification of this uniformity via conventional EDS is intrinsically limited by the severe energy overlap between N-Kα and Ti-L peaks [ 63 ], the inference of a macroscopically uniform nitrogen solid solution is well-supported by the highly symmetric XRD diffraction peaks adhering to Vegard’s law in Fig.  2  [ 64 ].

Furthermore, the exothermic reaction of 2Ti + N 2  → 2TiN (ΔH = − 337.6 kJ/mol) [ 65 ] releases additional heat, while a trace of in-situ formed TiN exhibits higher laser absorptivity than pure titanium [ 40 ]. These synergistic effects, namely plasma-enhanced coupling, exothermic heat, and improved absorptivity, collectively elevate the effective energy density and temperature of the molten pool. The intensified visible emission, meanwhile, originates from the metal vapor plume and spattering. Increased molten-pool temperature and nitrogen-augmented vapor pressure jointly amplify the recoil pressure that ejects metallic plumes and stabilizes keyhole cavities [ 66 ].

Fig. 7 Coaxial MPM results of molten pools under different atmospheres. (A physical quantity named absorption coefficient is defined as the ratio of laser power to reflected light to make a side-by-side comparison of laser absorptivity.)

High-fidelity simulations were performed to further analyze the influence of nitrogen on molten-pool dynamics. Figure  8 b reveals an increased molten-pool depth and an enhanced energy deposition under nitrogen-containing atmospheres, aligning with the elevated temperature observed via MPM (Fig.  7 ) and the morphology of single-track pools (Fig.  8 a). While the single-time absorptivity ( η ) increases, the effective energy absorptivity that incorporates multiple reflections reaches a plateau above 5 vol% N 2  (Fig.  8 c). This saturation is attributed to excessive pool deepening, which induces localized absorptivity heterogeneity and promotes keyhole instability, as evidenced by increased porosity in Fig.  S5 . Unstable keyhole dynamics reduce practical laser reflections, offsetting gains from higher  η . Consequently, a nitrogen concentration of 5 vol% is identified as optimal, striking a balance between improved energy‑utilization efficiency and preserved keyhole stability. This conclusion is further corroborated by the elevated recoil pressure observed under these conditions (Fig.  8 d). Notably, the actual porosity (Fig.  S5 ) in multi-layer builds is lower than in single-track simulations (Fig.  8 b), which is likely attributed to the effect of thermal-cycle remelting [ 67 ].

The intensified spattering stems from the synergy of enhanced recoil pressure and Marangoni-driven instability. Nitrogen addition elevates vapor pressure, thereby intensifying jet velocities and inducing surface collapse [ 68 ,  69 ]. Simultaneously, nitrogen acts as a surfactant to reduce surface tension [ 70 ] and disrupts the inherent Ti Marangoni flow (d σ /d T  < 0) [ 71 ,  72 ]. This reduction in surface tension lowers the critical velocity threshold for droplet detachment [ 73 ], thereby facilitating spatter generation.

where  c N  is the atomic percentage of nitrogen. Equation (8) captures anisotropic lattice expansion in α′-Ti from nitrogen incorporation, revealing that the  c -axis expansion (Δ c /Δ c N  = 0.0085 Å/at%) significantly exceeds the  a -axis expansion (Δ a /Δ c N  = 0.0008 Å/at%). This aligns with first-principles predictions of octahedral interstitial occupancy in HCP titanium, where nitrogen atoms (radius = 0.71 Å) prefer octahedral sites (radius = 0.61 Å) over tetrahedral voids (radius = 0.33 Å) [ 74 ]. The resultant anisotropic lattice distortion arises from asymmetric strain fields during octahedral site occupation, as atomic dimensions of nitrogen exceed the ideal interstitial radius by ~ 16%, necessitating coordinated atomic displacement [ 75 ]. Such interstitial solid-solution formation, accompanied by lattice-parameter evolution in Fig.  9 d, provides critical mechanistic insights into atmosphere-mediated strengthening of L-PBFed titanium alloys.

sections.heading: Effects of nitrogen on the microstructure evolution
paragraphs: From the phase morphology in Fig.  3 , the evolution mechanism is a thermally activated cascade [ 46 ]. At T max  > T L  (liquidus temperature), rapid cooling promotes coarse-columnar primary α′-martensite. Partial α′ reverts to β during interlayer remelting (T β  < T max  < T L ), and subsequent cooling initiates primary α′ from liquid and secondary α′ from residual β. At moderate peak temperature (M S  < T max  < T β ), the prior α′-martensite partially reverts to metastable β-phase and transforms to tertiary α′-martensite upon cooling [ 76 ]. Finally, the limited reverse transformation of existing martensite occurs under steep gradients, followed by cooling to quaternary α′-martensite at T max  < M S . This multiscale martensitic hierarchy arises from cyclic thermal stresses and non-isothermal kinetics inherent to µ-LPBF.

where  G  indicates the temperature gradient,  R  is the growth rate, and  D  represents the diffusion coefficient. Under similar thermal conditions (comparable G/R), the significantly larger  Q  value due to nitrogen addition greatly increases the critical threshold on the right-hand side of Eq. ( 10 ). Consequently, the solidification conditions tend to fall into the unstable regime, indicating that a substantial constitutional supercooling zone has high potential to form ahead of the solid–liquid interface. Mechanistically, the combination of this possible supercooled zone and the high  Q  value retard the growth velocity of the primary columnar dendrites. Such suppression of the columnar front provides a critical time window and sufficient undercooling for the emergence and development of random crystals preceding the moving boundary, thereby facilitating the microstructural shift from directional elongation to an isotropic equiaxed structure [ 81 ].

In addition to thermodynamic growth restriction, nitrogen promotes the CET effect through two potential auxiliary mechanisms. First, transient TiN particles are likely formed during processing and act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for new grains before dissolving upon cyclic reheating [ 82 ,  83 ]. This transient cascade is supported by a cross-scale evidentiary loop: the unremelted top surfaces exhibit both a characteristic golden-yellow luster and weak TiN diffraction peaks, whereas bulk XRD shows the complete absence of nitrides. Second, nitrogen-modified molten-pool convection can disrupt the epitaxial growth of columnar β-grains. Beyond initiating refinement of µ-LPBF, nitrogen stabilizes the fine microstructure by retarding grain coarsening via Zener pinning from any residual nitrides and solute-drag effects from nitrogen in solid solution, which collectively hinder grain boundary migration [ 84 ,  85 ,  86 – 87 ]. The microstructural evolution of µ-LPBFed TA15 under nitrogen is schematized in Fig.  10 . The hierarchical α′-martensite results from the cyclic thermal history of layer‑by‑layer deposition. During solidification, nitrogen promotes the CET of prior‑β grains by enhancing growth restriction and constitutional supercooling. Additional contributions may include heterogeneous nucleation on locally formed nitrides and modified melt‑pool convection. Post‑solidification grain refinement is further assisted by the geometric constraint of the equiaxed β‑grain network, possible Zener pinning from nitrides, and solute drag exerted by nitrogen in solid solution.

sections.heading: Effects of nitrogen on the mechanical properties
paragraphs: Fig. 12 Comparison between calculated and experimental yield strength of as-fabricated specimens under different atmospheres

The marginal  ε f  loss in the 5% N 2  specimen is mainly attributed to the activation of complementary strain-accommodation mechanisms. Dislocation glide within polygonized substructures, and the presence of LAGBs permits slip transfer, sustaining plasticity [ 96 ,  97 ]. Meanwhile, the formation of deformation twinning reorients the lattice and increases the Schmid factor for basal and prismatic slip systems (Fig.  S7 ), mitigating strain localization and delaying the exhaustion of slip systems [ 98 ]. The interaction of these in-situ twins with dislocation structures further enhances plasticity. Importantly, an obvious reduction in plasticity observed at higher nitrogen levels occurs despite the absence of TiN precipitates in bulk samples. This indicates that plasticity loss is primarily dictated by excessive solute nitrogen concentration rather than by brittle-phase precipitation, as reported [ 36 ,  50 ]. Specifically, as shown in Table  3 , the  c / a  ratio increases from 1.5938 to 1.6019 with nitrogen addition. Such a high ratio intrinsically limits crystal plasticity by increasing the critical resolved shear stress disparity between different slip systems, particularly hindering the activation of pyramidal < c + a> slip which is essential for c-axis strain accommodation [ 99 ]. Coupled with nitrogen-induced molten pool instability, this intrinsic lattice distortion dominates embrittlement at high nitrogen concentrations.

Beyond the specific case of the near-α TA15 alloy investigated here, the fundamental mechanisms driven by in-situ nitrogen microalloying hold profound broader implications for the reactive additive manufacturing of other titanium alloy systems. A notorious challenge in the L-PBF of most titanium alloys is the strong epitaxial growth of prior β-columnar grains, which inevitably leads to severe mechanical anisotropy. Because almost all commercial titanium alloys undergo solidification via the high-temperature β-phase field [ 100 ], the nitrogen-induced high growth restriction factor and the consequent constitutional supercooling elucidated in this work can serve as a universal metallurgical toolkit to promote the CET of parent β-grains across various Ti systems. Furthermore, the coordinated “Solid Solution + Recovery” pathway provides a highly transferable, post-processing-free strategy for other α-containing titanium alloys to achieve superior mechanical properties. Ultimately, manipulating reactive mixed-gas atmospheres establishes a general framework for dynamically tailoring molten-pool thermophysics, overcoming mechanical anisotropy, and optimizing hierarchical substructures across the broader family of advanced reactive alloys.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this work, a high-performance TA15 alloy is fabricated via µ-LPBF, employing a reactive atmosphere to induce in-situ nitrogen microalloying. The principal conclusions can be summarized as follows:

The synergistic interplay between nitrogen addition and µ-LPBF significantly enhances isotropic mechanical response. Under 5 vol% N 2 , the specimen achieved a  σ max  of 2266 MPa, surpassing values reported for modified TC4 and TA15, while maintaining minimal loss of deformability. In terms of molten-pool dynamics and process stability, nitrogen addition increases energy absorption, elevating molten-pool temperature and depth. However, excessive nitrogen leads to keyhole instability driven by high recoil pressure, causing porosity and spattering. A critical balance between energy coupling efficiency and keyhole stability is identified at 5 vol% N 2 , ensuring dense fabrication. Regarding microstructural evolution, the elimination of anisotropy stems from the enhanced growth restriction factor ( Q ) induced by nitrogen. Nitrogen enrichment generates significant constitutional supercooling, promoting the CET of the parent β-grains. This morphological transformation effectively eliminates the crystallographic texture and induces mechanical isotropy. The superior mechanical performance is governed by a “Solid Solution + Recovery” pathway. While interstitial nitrogen induces severe lattice distortion as the primary strengthening source, the dense dislocation networks undergo in-situ polygonization to form LAGBs, which further facilitate twin nucleation via partial dislocation emission. These hierarchical substructures effectively impede dislocation motion, providing critical strain accommodation and ensuring ultra-high strength without premature failure.

Significantly, this work establishes an integrated framework combining high-fidelity simulation,  in‑situ  monitoring, and multi‑scale characterization for reactive µ‑LPBF of Ti alloys. It bridges theory and experiment under mixed‑gas atmospheres, overcoming mechanical anisotropy and delivering high performance without complex post‑processing, thereby providing a practical toolkit for defect‑free additive manufacturing of advanced materials. While the current mechanistic study and multidirectional compressive evaluations robustly validate the microstructural isotropy and strengthening pathways for compression-dominated micro-architectures, the translation of this reactive strategy to upscaled L-PBF systems for comprehensive macroscopic tensile and fatigue assessments represents a critical avenue for future structural engineering.
